items.title: First Liberty: Minnesota County Has ‘Essentially Criminalized Being Amish’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The Amish community in Minnesota is pushing back amid claims of unfair government policies that purportedly fail to offer religious accommodations — and even reportedly led to one Amish man’s arrest.

First Liberty attorney Ryan Gardner said his firm is representing two Amish congregations in Mille Lacs County, Minnesota, arguing the county itself has “essentially criminalized being Amish.”

“As you might know, the Amish community lives by a pretty strict set of religious principles, and many of those involve not being involved in technology,” Gardner said. “And kind of keeping to themselves … they want to be able to live according to their religious beliefs, and a lot of what those beliefs require, frankly … to be set apart from modern society.”

According to First Liberty, problems began for these congregations during COVID-19, when county officials reportedly implemented a new permitting system for building structures and homes.

“It went from a paper form to an electronic form,” Gardner said. “As you might imagine, the Amish don’t really use electronic forms or the internet, so this was a significant problem, and they had no alternative for a long time.”

With no other option for simply getting clearance to build homes, he said “a lot of the people in these congregations just proceeded to build anyways because they didn’t have a choice.”

Gardner said Mille Lacs County did eventually change the policy to make a paper option available, but added there is an additional $50 fee for requesting permitting on paper.

“Pretty much the only people who are actually using that are the Amish, and so now they’re having to pay a special fee just to even start the permitting process,” the lawyer said. “And once they get in, there are more problems because they’re trying to impose all kinds of modern requirements that are just inconsistent with the Amish way of life.”

Gardner said officials have been so hard on the Amish that they even put one man in jail “for the crime of building and living in his home.”

“This particular individual had been living in his home for something like five years and then, suddenly, he’s criminally cited for it, and he goes to court, and he’s convicted,” the lawyer said. “And he is … immediately taken to jail.”

Gardner said it is “ludicrous” and “extreme” to prosecute someone for such a “petty” offense, and added that such a reaction is rare. He added that the Amish had purportedly tried to go to the county to work the issue out but were “met with hostility.”

“Here’s the kicker in all of this,” he continued, “Built into the very ordinance that the county is enforcing here is a provision that gives the county discretion to give exemptions to these requirements to anybody that it wants.”

First Liberty sent a letter to the county recently demanding they stop enforcement actions against the Amish, especially considering warrants that are currently out for others. They’re also looking for an exemption that would settle the issue once and for all, noting that, from his perspective, the Amish build insanely safe structures.

Mille Lacs County told CBN News that lawyers cannot comment on ongoing cases.

items.title: 9/11 Survivor’s Chilling Warning About ‘Evil’ 25 Years Later
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A former Secret Service agent who survived the Sept. 11 terror attacks is warning that he believes some Americans might not be gleaning important lessons from the deadly assault.

Darin Kinder said he “had a front row seat to evil” that fateful day, but that he also “saw the best of America” amid the terror.

“I was outside when the second impact happened 80-90 yards from the base of that tower,” he said. “And then scurried up into World Trade Tower OneIwith some other coworkers, helping people evacuate.”

Then, he was at the base of Tower Two when it buckled and collapsed. It was in that moment that Kinder faced a harrowing situation, as he was in a battle for his life.

“That began my mad dash for life,” he said. “That’s when I thought it was gone for sure. I thought it was game over.”

Kinder tried to outrun the tower’s collapse, struggling to breathe through the thick smoke. He was able to survive and flee the chaos and has spent the past 25 years sharing his story. His memoir, “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11,” has been one of the tools he has used to offer up his journey toward hope and healing.

Among the other topics he covered is courage, something he described as “a choice.” And as Kinder reflects on the hope he experienced amid so much pain, he also has a warning for Americans 25 years after radical Islam inflicted such pain on the nation: that some might have forgotten what unfolded.

“I think a September 10th mindset is kind of encroaching in, and where we just want to keep our head buried in the sand and not address the real evil that’s there, the real presence of a threat that’s there,” Kinder said. “And we can’t have that.”

He said he’s been bothered and concerned by some of what he’s seen among young people who are asking questions to which they should know the answers. Tragically, he said many of these people simply haven’t been educated on these matters, with the facts of what unfolded at the hands of “19 radical Islamic terrorists” being shielded or ignored.

Kinder also said other historic elements surrounding the event that “killed nearly 3,000 Americans and that kicked off a generational war — the global War on Terror — that we have seen the negative ripple and ramifications of” have also been largely ignored. He encouraged people to adhere to the truth, and warned that some Christians are too focused on the wrong elements.

“It’s this devout devotion to the 11th Commandment — ‘Thou shall be nice,'” Kinder said. “And it’s just not there. I mean, we’re we’re commanded to speak the truth in love and truth without love is harsh. Love without truth is just trying to be a nice guy that gets along to go-a-long. We have to be able to to to relay the truth to the next generation.”

Kinder said it’s often a temptation for Christians to want to be comfortable, yet Scripture shows Jesus and his followers weren’t always in that position. In fact, they were “hunted…chased out of town” and even beaten and stoned.

“We want to embrace comfort and not have real conversations,” he said, noting that the history of Islam was one of imposition at its roots, juxtaposing it against Christianity, which he called a “religion of invitation.” Understanding these realities, he said, is key.

“I would just say bluntly that evil doesn’t stop when you ask nicely,” he said. “And when it reaches its radical form and it’s literally attacking you physically or it’s undercutting everything in your culture and everything in your society and slowly changing over time that needs to be pushed back.”

Kinder continued, “That is darkness, and we’re called to bring light into dark.”

He encouraged Christians to “get engaged” and to stop burying their heads in the sand. Read more of his story in “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11.”

items.title: ‘That’s Why I’m Not Scared of Death’: NBA Player Michael Porter Jr. Spent a Livestream Telling N3on Jesus Is the Only Way
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Michael Porter Jr. didn’t go on N3on’s stream to talk about God. Then the streamer brought up AI, and the conversation went somewhere else entirely. Porter, who led the Brooklyn Nets in scoring last season at a career-high 24.2 points a game, sat in on Mikyle Rafiq’s Kick livestrea
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Michael Porter Jr. didn’t go on N3on’s stream to talk about God. Then the streamer brought up AI, and the conversation went somewhere else entirely.

Porter, who led the Brooklyn Nets in scoring last season at a career-high 24.2 points a game, sat in on Mikyle Rafiq’s Kick livestream for the better part of Tuesday. Rafiq, who streams as N3on and has more than a million followers on both YouTube and Instagram, said he was worried about where AI is headed. Porter’s answer skipped the technology.

“The world’s just, it’s evil, bro,” he said. “That’s why just make sure you’re right with God, man. Not just any God. Make sure you’re right with Jesus Christ.”

Rafiq said he’s Muslim, respects every religion and tells his viewers to pray to one God. Porter asked what happens if they’re praying to the wrong one.

“But everyone worships the same God, no?” Rafiq said.

“No,” Porter said.

He kept going. “Some people think that the best thing about this life is partying. Some people think the best part about this life is going on a walk with friends. Whatever you think that the point of this life is, there’s gotta be something better than this.”

Then he turned it around. “Are you scared of death?”

“I’m so scared of death,” Rafiq said. “That’s my number one fear.”

Porter told him about a Muslim Uber driver he once asked how he knew he was going to heaven. “He was like, ‘None of us do. We just try to live our best and be a good person, and then we’re all scared, and then we die, and we cross our fingers.'”

“Christianity’s the only religion where it’s like none of us can be good enough to go to heaven, ’cause we’ve all sinned. We’ve all done bad things, and someone else came and died for us and forgave us of our sins. That’s why I’m so secure in the fact that I’m going to heaven, and that’s why I’m not scared of death.”

“Someone else did it for me. Jesus died on the cross for us, dog.”

A few minutes later he invited Rafiq to come to church with him.

Porter has never been quiet about this. He grew up in a devout family in Missouri, won a title with the Nuggets in 2023 and was traded to Brooklyn last summer, where he became the Nets’ best player.

The stream ran almost six hours. This was the part people clipped.

items.title: Sin and Redemption in Craig Finn’s Little Worlds
items.author: Eric Cyr
items.summary:
Eric Cyr

His conversion and his life are still imperfect, but Finn gives us a vision not only of sin but of hope.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Eric Cyr

In his essay “On Fairy-stories,” J. R. R. Tolkien famously referred to his creative work, and the human creative act more generally, as “sub-creation.” That is, only God can properly be called a creator, the Creator ex nihilo, and none of us under God’s dominion have the power to truly create. Instead, we “sub-create,” working with the materials of God’s handiwork, becoming in Tolkien’s words the “little makers” of our own little worlds, like a child at play with the toys his father has given him.

Tolkien may seem a strange starting point to talk about the songs of an indie rocker, but Craig Finn is something of a strange figure in the world of pop and indie songwriters. Finn doesn’t invent new worlds or languages like Tolkien does, doesn’t insert any magical creatures into his songs, but he creates—or sub-creates—entire lives and the worlds that surround them in miniature. He sketches characters and stories over the span of four or five minutes with the same care and attention of a model world builder.

Frequently, these songs stand alone, but on his most recent album, Always Been, Finn has created a larger world that compounds and expands song by song around its narrator. Like most of Finn’s characters, this narrator is broken, bruised, and down on his luck: a failed preacher and husband who talks about how he became a reverend despite his lack of faith, met his wife in his congregation, and his depression and falling away from both his wife and church. His story is fleshed out in an accumulation of details that builds his world in pieces throughout the album. We learn in “A Man Needs a Vocation,” for example, more about how he became a pastor. Sleeping in his car, he finds a pamphlet on his windshield advertising a cheap twenty-week course in divinity where

He memorized the sacred texts
That earned him the certificate
That led him a place to live
And though he didn’t believe in it
He was quite convinced
A man needs a vocation

The greatest strength of Finn’s writing is his particularity: his ability to write sharply observed, crystalline lines that are both unexpected and perfectly capture some truth. In “The Man I’ve Always Been,” the narrator describes himself as

The guy who’s trying not to cry
In the supermarket aisle
Confused why there’s so many types of juice

Finn’s narrator could tell us (and Dana, his ex-wife to whom the song is addressed) more straightforwardly that he still gets overwhelmed and depressed sometimes. But the specificity of confusion over so many types of juice makes the point more powerfully, viscerally. The listener feels a more particularized embarrassment for him, imagining him standing there in the juice aisle, shopping basket in one hand, the other hand covering his face, crying as a woman tries to reach past him for a bottle of orange juice. We feel the specific empathy of imagining ourselves in that aisle, perhaps thinking to ourselves, “I, too, have been overwhelmed by too many options at the supermarket. I, too, have become emotional and embarrassed in a public place.” All of these aspects work together subconsciously to give the line its emotive power.

“People of Substance” begins:

Dana, I don’t get depressed anymore
Except possibly December at the Delaware shore
Or maybe missing numbers on the motel doors
The toy section at the drugstore

Again, each highly specific line implies a depth of reality and history that reverberates beyond the detail itself. What happened in December on the Delaware shore that triggers depression for him? Why the toy section? Regret at not having children, perhaps, or at least a reminder of the lost possibilities? And even in that line, notice that it’s the toy section specifically at the drugstore, which is typically a cheap and limited toy section compared to those at a big box store or mom and pop toy store. This points out that he’s spending time at the drugstore, possibly for prescriptions for his depression, or for what else we’re not sure. In any event, we don’t associate the drugstore with things going particularly well. So much life and implication are compressed into the line. And in this song, the second on the album, “missing numbers on the motel doors” doesn’t mean much to the listener specifically. But later in the album, we hear about a motel in Washington state and a tragic episode there. The missing numbers end up being a hint dropped early in the album that expands and takes on greater significance later on. This is the micro-level world-building that Finn accomplishes throughout his songs.

Every song on the album could yield examples of this, but I’ll give just one more. The opening song, “Bethany,” features a final verse that expertly blends implication and concrete description in the accumulation of small, well-chosen details:

The devil came in hot
Someone called the cops
I explained to them how much it is you mean to me

The cuffs they made a click
As they wrapped around my wrists
Everybody’s got their version of security

Maybe there’s a life where
The Reverend has his wife
And Jesus has his ministry in Galilee

But the sunset looks like blood
From the window of the bus
Somewhere between Harrisburg and Bethany

The listener experiences here a balance between strong imagery and evocative, less-is-more lines that imply the reverberations of a larger world.

Though the album’s narrator is nondenominational, Finn himself is Catholic—he’s spoken about how formative his Catholicism was when he was young and about returning to the Church in his thirties after falling away from it in his college years. He writes within a cosmology of original and personal sin, of brokenness and our fallen state, but with an affection for his characters and an eye turned toward redemption.

In “I Walk With a Cane,” Finn digs more explicitly than elsewhere into his vision of fallen man as the narrator sings:

The stone in my shoe just reminds me
We’re all born with original sin
 . . .
It’s really hard to walk when you’re carrying this cross
To remind you of your greatest sin

Whether or not this was Finn’s intent, the stone in his shoe alludes to one of Catholic fiction’s greatest writers, Flannery O’Connor. O’Connor had a complete artistic vision of fallen humanity and the work of divine grace in the lowest, most broken moments of man. In Wise Blood, after everything in Hazel Motes’s life falls apart, after all his failed attempts to run away from God and start a “Church of Christ without Christ,” he repents in his own broken way and fills his shoes with stones as a penance. In his own story-songs, Finn participates in this tradition of Catholic writers who recognize man’s brokenness at its extremes but still have hope for redemption.

And for the narrator of Always Been, the stone in his shoe is not the final act. In the next song, “Clayton,” we hear that:

I took Clayton as a name
The day they said that I was saved
They said the Lord just reached his hands out and
Formed me out of clay

This faithless former preacher’s life hits such a low of brokenness and fault that he realizes he needs something else. He sees himself as newly formed and sings, “I finally took the stone out of my shoe.” His conversion and his life are still imperfect, but here, Finn gives us a vision not only of sin but of hope. He gives his sub-created world a cosmology of redemption, reflecting the presence of a God who loves us even in our brokenness, but who desires to bring us out of our sin and into union with him.
